en.title: Netanyahu weighs military action against Iran while government serves in caretaker capacity
en.dek: Netanyahu's caretaker government considers military action against Iran despite US and military opposition
facts: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government is in caretaker capacity after losing its majority in last month's parliamentary elections.,Al Jazeera reports caretaker status continues until a new governing majority is formed.

Article 30 of Israel's Basic Law states an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.,Al Jazeera cites the Basic Law as the source for caretaker authority.
Netanyahu has been calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran.,Israel's Ynet News reports on the calls.
The Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran.,Channel 13 reported the assessment was presented to Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot.

Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir said Pakistan aims to become a competitive destination for long-term mineral investment at the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026.,Dawn reports Munir's remarks at the forum.
body:
Al Jazeera reports that despite losing its majority in last month's parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government remains in power in a caretaker capacity until a new governing majority is formed, a process that could take months as Israel's opposition struggles to form a coalition.
Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and politicians vying to replace him.
On Wednesday, the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran, according to public broadcaster KAN.
However, Israel's Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent, a principle known as the duty of restraint, Al Jazeera reports.
Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University London, told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as urgent and in the national interest.
Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told Reuters that security issues are generally the clearest exception to a caretaker government's duty of restraint, and that the Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war.

The Israeli military establishment assessed there is no urgent need to attack Iran, according to Channel 13. This assessment was presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot during a briefing on Wednesday.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government's caretaker status raises the political burden of proof for such a decision, saying Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government.
On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation, though US Central Command later dismissed the reports as mere speculation.
en.context: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leads a caretaker government following parliamentary elections and is reportedly considering military action against Iran. The Israeli military establishment assesses there is no urgent need for such action, while the security cabinet has ordered preparations for an attack. Opinions differ on whether a caretaker government has the authority to initiate war.
